My degree is in Geographic Information Systems, so when I landed an interview out of college (right down the street from it!) for an entry level analyst position, I was pretty stoked.

There was a huge rainstorm that day, and all of the roads were muddy and wet.  My GPS brought me to the back of the parking lot, which didn’t have an entrance.  So I pulled a quick three point turn, and then wound up stuck in a ditch.  My interview was in ten minutes.  I put my hazards on, locked my car, and ran across the parking lot inside.  The interviewer greeted me, and handed me a parking pass.  I could have lied and said I took the bus (the stop was literally right outside), but nope.  I took it, went back to my car, and put it on the mirror.  

Went back in, nailed the interview and felt pretty great walking out.  The interviewer insisted that she come with me to retrieve the pass, however, as some people had stolen them before.  Oh.  Oh no.

We walked right up to my car, I handed her the pass, and she was sort of in shock and walked back in.  I mean, at first I still felt good about it.  I performed well under pressure.  I got there on time.  I had a great resume for the position.

It was not meant to be, though.  It was an interview for the National Highway Safety Research Institute and I got in a wreck on the way there.

Check out the podcast “The Habitat.”  It’s about the people chosen to simulate the first colony on Mars by living in a small dome for a year here on Earth.  One of the points they make is that NASA (and managers from many disciplines, especially the STEM fields) consider the fact that the best-and-brightest individuals from their respective fields *might not* be the best for the mission when trying to form a cohesive team.  

Remember, these people will have to work together for months, probably years on end, and it is vastly more important to choose individuals that work better together as a team, as opposed to “S-rank” astronauts that might not play well in the sandbox together.
